definition.text: A market-based system of debits and credits, used mainly in the United States, in which wetlands are restored, created or enhanced to make up for unavoidable damage to wetlands elsewhere.

facts.text: Mitigation banks are sites where wetland projects are carried out before the damage they compensate for; their results become credits that developers can buy.
It grew from compensatory mitigation under section 404 of the US Clean Water Act, aiming at "no net loss of wetlands".
The first wetland mitigation banks were set up in the early 1980s following 1983 guidance from the US Fish and Wildlife Service.
Regulators often require more habitat than is damaged, a mitigation ratio, which serves the public interest.
Credits are released in stages as a bank meets performance milestones over an establishment period of about 10 to 12 years.
By 2024 more than 1200 mitigation banks were operating in the US, with 750,000 credits approved.
Studies suggest a significant share of compensation sites fail to meet administrative and ecological performance standards.

definition.text: Measures that restore, create, enhance or preserve wetlands to make up for damage that cannot be avoided; the US term for biodiversity offsetting.

facts.text: It applies only after the mitigation sequence of avoid, minimise, then compensate has been followed.
It can be on-site, on or next to the damaged area, or off-site.
Besides banks, it can be done through in-lieu fee programmes, where permittees pay into an approved fund, or permittee-responsible projects, where they do and answer for the work themselves.
Revised US rules in 2008 made mitigation banks the preferred method of compensatory mitigation.

definition.text: A voluntary legal agreement between a landowner and a government agency or conservation group that restricts future development on a site, setting it aside permanently for conservation.

facts.text: In the US, land used for mitigation banking must be protected by a conservation easement.
The commitment binds future owners of the land, and a trust fund may pay for long-term management.
Landowners may see the permanent restriction as a drawback because it limits future uses and can lower land value.

title: Conservation banking

definition.text: A market-based method of offsetting harm to threatened or endangered species protected under the US Endangered Species Act by creating conservation banks.

facts.text: Conservation banks are permanently protected parcels of land managed to keep endangered species and their habitat alive.
Developers who must harm protected species can buy credits from a bank instead of protecting small patches themselves.
Pooling mitigation into larger reserves gives better habitat and connectivity than small isolated patches, and is cheaper to maintain.
California created the first conservation bank in 1995 and leads with over 30; the nation's 130 banks protect over 160,000 acres.
Credit prices are set largely by supply and demand and range from $1500 for a Gopher Tortoise to $325,000 for vernal pool preservation.
Unlike wetland mitigation banking, conservation banking does not require no net loss.

notes: Conservation banking lead says its intention is no net loss (b464313919bb), while Biodiversity banking says it does not require no net loss (8b3b265c21cf); verification pass may want to look. Also: origin given as 'wetland mitigation banks created in the early 1990s' (dfd9181798ea) vs 1980s on Mitigation banking page.

title: Biodiversity Impact Credit

definition.text: A transferable biodiversity credit designed to reduce the global risk of species extinction.

facts.text: Its metric, developed by academics at Queen Mary University of London and Bar-Ilan University, measures how interventions change the average long-term survival chances of species.
For each species it adds up the change in global population divided by the current population, so restoring one threatened species from near zero gives about one credit.
It targets Target 4 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework on cutting extinction risk, and the TNFD recommends its use.
Critics of biodiversity credits say monetising nature oversimplifies it and that credits can be used for greenwashing or merely to offset damage.

contested_note: Critics say pricing nature through credits oversimplifies it and invites greenwashing, while proponents point to growing private investment.
